#8827. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

The Smith machine sometimes gets a bad rap, but it can be a solid addition to any home gym.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Nov 2, 2026

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester says. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he says the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”

The G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

For less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester says.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

“This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

Don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

We rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

Like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester says.

As for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”

At about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”

Before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

However, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

Unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” says Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, new lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

“Maintaining correct form is important for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”

The guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he says.

If you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” says Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”

You won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” says Maietta.

What should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:

Consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

If you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

Smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

## Flying Qatar QSuites for 70,000 Miles: The Redemption That Feels Impossible Until You Do It Imagine settling into your own private suite — a door that actually closes, a fully flat bed measuring 80 inches long, a 21.5-inch 4K screen, and a meal service that rivals the best business-class restaurants at 40,000 feet. Qatar Airways QSuites isn't just the best business class product in the sky right now; it's the product that frequent flyers describe as the moment they understood why people obsess over travel rewards. And you can book it for 70,000 American AAdvantage miles one-way. Let that sink in. The same seat — Washington Dulles to Doha, with the ability to continue to dozens of destinations across Asia, Africa, and beyond — retails for **$5,000 to $9,000 in cash**. At 70,000 AAdvantage miles, you're extracting between **7.1 and 12.9 cents per point**. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This redemption is *three to six times that*. This is what the FI community means when we talk about travel rewards as a genuine wealth multiplier. If you've been stockpiling points wondering whether they're actually worth something, this is your answer. A cash ticket that costs more than many people's monthly take-home salary becomes nearly free with the right points strategy. The inefficiency exists because AAdvantage still prices partner awards — flights on airlines like Qatar, JAL, and Cathay Pacific — on a **fixed partner award chart** rather than the dynamic pricing it uses for American-operated flights. Qatar, as a oneworld alliance member, is required to make award space available to partner programs. American prices that space at a flat 70,000 miles for business class, regardless of what Qatar itself charges in cash or its own Avios currency. The result is a structural arbitrage opportunity: you're using a fixed-price chart to book a premium product that Qatar prices at whatever the market will bear — and the market bears a *lot* for QSuites. The ChooseFI community has long understood that the highest-leverage use of points isn't domestic economy upgrades. It's premium international cabin redemptions where the gap between cash price and points cost is widest. On that spectrum, QSuites via AAdvantage sits near the very top.

The core insight here is understanding two separate pricing systems operating simultaneously. Qatar Airways prices its QSuites cabin dynamically in cash — demand surges around holidays, business travel seasons, and major events can push that $5,000 base price to $9,000 or beyond. But American AAdvantage doesn't care about any of that. As a oneworld alliance partner, AAdvantage uses a fixed partner award chart for Qatar redemptions: 70,000 miles one-way in business class, full stop.

This means the more expensive the cash ticket gets, the better your CPP becomes — without you doing anything differently. Book during peak travel periods when cash prices spike to $9,000, and you're extracting 12.9 cents per AAdvantage mile. Even at the floor — a $5,000 cash ticket — you're at 7.1 cents per point. Both numbers are extraordinary.

AAdvantage periodically runs "Web Specials" — discounted partner awards where pricing drops significantly below the standard chart. On Qatar routes, these have historically appeared at 50,000 miles one-way for business class. At 50K miles against a $5,000 cash ticket, your CPP jumps to 10 cents per point. These specials are unpredictable and availability is limited, but if you're flexible on travel dates, checking AA.com regularly for Web Specials on Qatar routes can yield an even better deal.

AAdvantage doesn't have a direct credit card transfer relationship with most major bank currencies the way Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards do. Your primary transfer paths are:

One of the most important nuances of this redemption: AAdvantage has a low fuel surcharge policy. When you book Qatar metal through AAdvantage, you pay government taxes and carrier fees, but AAdvantage does not pass through the fuel surcharges that Qatar would charge if you booked through its own program. This can save hundreds of dollars compared to booking QSuites through Avios or Qatar Privilege Club directly. Always verify fees at checkout, but expect to pay $50–$150 in fees rather than the $500+ you might see through other programs.

Doha isn't just a destination — it's Qatar's hub, and connecting through DOH opens the entire Qatar network. A flight to DOH becomes a connection point for onward travel to destinations across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the Indian Subcontinent, and East Africa, all on the same premium aircraft and the same 70,000-mile award. The IAD→DOH route is one of the best-documented entry points into this system.

Compare this to AA's own Flagship Business product on the same routes (which often prices at 60,000-85,000 miles with dynamic pricing) and you are getting a dramatically superior product — QSuites — for a comparable or lower mileage cost. Let's run the numbers on a concrete example.

The Route: Washington Dulles (IAD) to Doha (DOH) on Qatar Airways QR 22, operating a Boeing 777-300ER with QSuites. This is a nonstop flight of approximately 13 hours — exactly the kind of long-haul journey where your seat product matters enormously.

The Cash Price: A business class ticket on this route typically runs $5,500 to $7,500, and during peak travel windows — think spring break, summer, or major holidays — it can reach $9,000. Call it a realistic average of $6,500.

The Points Cost: 70,000 AAdvantage miles + approximately $80–$120 in taxes and fees.

The Math: At $6,500 cash value against 70,000 miles, you're getting 9.3 cents per point. Against a $9,000 peak ticket, you're at 12.9 cents per point. Either way, this is among the highest-value AAdvantage redemptions available anywhere in the program.

You arrive at Dulles and proceed to the Qatar Airways check-in counter, where you're processed as a business class passenger. At Doha, you'll have access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world, featuring a full à la carte restaurant, shower suites, and a calm, spacious environment that makes a layover feel genuinely pleasant.

Onboard, your QSuite is a private cabin with a door that slides closed. The bed extends to a full 80 inches. You'll be offered a genuine dine-on-demand service — no scheduled meal times, no "chicken or pasta" announcements over the intercom. The wine list is serious. The bedding is from The White Company. The 21.5-inch screen is 4K.

For the ChooseFI community, the most powerful part of this isn't the luxury itself — it's the ratio. You're experiencing a $6,500–$9,000 product for the cost of points you earned on everyday spending and a small tax outlay. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: maximum experience per dollar (or point) deployed.

Do this: Book as far out as possible. AAdvantage allows bookings up to 331 days in advance. Qatar releases its best award inventory to partner programs at the time of schedule opening — not closer to departure. If you have a target travel window, search at the 331-day mark. Availability genuinely deteriorates as departure approaches.

Do this: Watch for Web Special pricing drops. AAdvantage's Web Specials have historically offered Qatar business class awards at 50,000 miles instead of the standard 70,000. These appear without warning on aa.com under the "Web Specials" tab. If you're flexible with your dates within a week or two, checking this section regularly (or signing up for AAdvantage email alerts) can save you 20,000 miles — a meaningful difference.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou for same-day transfers. If you find award space and need to transfer points immediately, Citi ThankYou → AAdvantage transfers are instant. This is the fastest transfer path and eliminates the risk of space disappearing while your transfer processes. Keep Citi points in reserve as your QSuites "strike fund."

Avoid this: Transferring Marriott points unless absolutely necessary. The Marriott Bonvoy → AAdvantage transfer at 3:1 is deeply inefficient. You're spending three Marriott points to create one AAdvantage mile. Marriott points are worth roughly 0.7–0.8 cents each, meaning you're paying effectively 2.1–2.4 cents per AAdvantage mile — still potentially worth it for QSuites, but exhaust your Citi and Bilt options first.

Do this: Treat DOH as a hub, not a destination. Doha is Qatar's base, meaning a 70,000-mile award from the US to DOH can be the first leg of an onward journey to destinations across Asia, South Asia, or East Africa — all on Qatar metal. A trip from IAD to Singapore (SIN) routing through DOH, for example, puts you in QSuites for the transatlantic leg and potentially a narrowbody for the shorter DOH-SIN segment.

Avoid this: Booking round-trip when one-way is more flexible. AAdvantage allows one-way partner awards. Book your outbound and return separately — this dramatically expands your availability options and lets you mix partners or return on a different airline without being locked into a single itinerary.

Do this: Build AAdvantage miles through Bilt's monthly rent payments. Bilt Rewards is the only major program that earns points on rent. If you're paying $1,500–$2,500/month in rent, a year of Bilt earning generates 18,000–30,000 Bilt points — transferable to AAdvantage at 1:1. That's a meaningful contribution to your 70,000-mile target from a spend category you have anyway.

This redemption is purpose-built for the serious couple or solo traveler with a specific long-haul itinerary in mind — a honeymoon, a milestone anniversary trip, a once-in-a-while splurge that you've decided to fund with points rather than cash. Minimum requirements: 70,000 AAdvantage miles per person, plus $80–$150 in cash for taxes and fees. You also need the patience and flexibility to find saver award space, which is the primary friction in this redemption.

## Honest Difficulty Assessment: Moderate This redemption scores **moderate difficulty** — and that rating is accurate. It's not a click-and-book process like domestic awards, but it's not the multi-step puzzle that some ultra-premium redemptions require either. The difficulty is concentrated in **two specific areas**. **Challenge #1: Finding Available Award Space** Qatar releases QSuites award inventory to AAdvantage, but not generously. Availability scores a **2 out of 5**, which means you will sometimes search for weeks before finding the right date. This is the primary bottleneck. The fix: search early (331 days out), be flexible within a 1-2 week window, and use ExpertFlyer alerts to get notified when space opens. Midweek departures and shoulder-season travel windows (late January through March, September through November) tend to surface more space. **Challenge #2: Building 70,000 AAdvantage Miles** AAdvantage's transfer partner list is narrower than Chase or Amex ecosystems. Your best paths are Citi ThankYou (instant transfers) and Bilt Rewards (1-2 days). This earns a **3 out of 5** for ease of earning — achievable, but requires intentional card strategy rather than casual accumulation. **The booking process itself** — once you have miles and availability — is straightforward on aa.com. AAdvantage's award search tool clearly displays partner availability and pricing. **The encouragement:** Every traveler in the ChooseFI community who has navigated this redemption consistently describes it as worth every minute of the search process. The moment that QSuite door closes, you'll understand exactly why. If you're willing to invest the time to find availability and build your miles intentionally, this redemption is entirely within reach — and the payoff is extraordinary.

Log into your AAdvantage account and search for one-way business class flights on your desired route. Filter for partner-operated flights and look specifically for Qatar Airways (QR) flight numbers. The search results will show the mileage cost alongside availability.

If aa.com does not show availability, search the same route on Qatar's own website using a Privilege Club account. Qatar sometimes releases space that AA's system takes 24-48 hours to reflect. If you find space on Qatar but not AA, check back the following day.

Not all Qatar business class flights operate QSuites. Check the aircraft type listed in the search results — A350-1000 and select 777-300ERs have QSuites. Verify on SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to ensure you are booking the premium product.

Once you confirm QSuites availability, complete the booking on aa.com using your AAdvantage miles. The process is the same as booking any AA award flight. You will see the mileage cost plus taxes and fees before confirming.

American Airlines charges approximately 70,000 AAdvantage miles one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights. Taxes and fees are typically $30 to $80. A round trip comes to roughly 140,000 miles total plus minimal fees.

Both options cost roughly 70,000 points one-way. The main differences are earning sources and booking experience. AAdvantage miles are earned through Citi cards and Bilt, while Avios can be earned through Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. AA offers web booking while BA may require phone calls. Check availability through both programs — they sometimes see different award space.

Yes. The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select earns bonus miles on purchases, Bilt Rewards transfers to AAdvantage at 1:1, AA's SimplyMiles program earns miles on everyday purchases linked to your credit card, and the AAdvantage shopping portal earns miles at online retailers. You can accumulate 70,000 or more miles without taking a single AA flight.

Airlines control how much award inventory they release to each partner. Qatar may release seats to BA's Avios program but not to AA, or vice versa. AA's search engine also has known inconsistencies with partner availability display. Always cross-reference qatarairways.com and ba.com if aa.com shows no availability on your desired dates.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Using AAdvantage miles for Qatar business class is one of the strongest partner award redemptions in the oneworld alliance. At 70,000 miles for a product that retails at $5,000 to $8,000, the value per mile is outstanding. The web-based booking experience on aa.com removes the friction of phone calls, and the lack of fuel surcharges keeps your cash outlay minimal. If you earn AAdvantage miles through Citi cards or Bilt transfers, this should be at the top of your aspirational redemption list. Search early, stay flexible on dates, and book the moment QSuites space appears.

On Episode 309 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev and Jose Raymond, and the panel discussed Shawn Clarida’s bright potential in the Open bodybuilding category.

Clarida is currently dipping his toes into the Open waters to great success. The man they call “The Giant Killer” stands a just 5 feet and 2 inches tall, but his lofty achievements include two Olympia titles in the 212 division. In 2026, Clarida qualified for both the Open and 212 divisions at the ‘O.’ But while he decided to stick with 212 and came second, he went on to win in 212 at the Italy Pro on October 25. He has also continued his ambitions in the Open division, placing first at the recent Poland Pro on October 31.

“Shinn is like almost perfect, in that little frame, in that little body,” said Raymond, discussing Clarida’s victory in Poland. “I would have given it to Shaun too,” agreed Dennis James. “Because he was the most complete guy in the stage. These other guys were taller and bigger than him, but when you look at bodybuilding, and you look for completeness, Shaun Clarida was clear and it wasn’t even close.”

The "Giant Killer" made great use of his training time in Japan.

The panel felt that had The Giant Killer entered the Open category in Slovakia, he could have beaten Michal Krizanek, who won the night. “Dude, I would probably pick Shaun over Krizo,” said Raymond.

Such a stamp of approval will come as great news for Clarida, because Krizanek placed a career high sixth place in the Open division at the 2026 Olympia. Could The Giant Killer really compete with the biggest bodies in Open bodybuilding?

“If you really ask me who is the better bodybuilder (compared to Krizo), I would pick Shaun,” said The Menace. “Yeah, he’s short, but he’s almost flawless,” he added.

“He’s got everything,” agreed Raymond. “Your eye goes to him.”

“One hundred percent,” concurred Milos Sarcev.

#8822. Thomas van Tonder Just Crossed Africa’s Highest Bridge, By Hand

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

If you’ve ever struggled to complete a set of money bars, spare a thought for obstacle course athlete, Thomas van Tonder, who just completed the kind of challenge that you have to see in order to believe it’s true: scaling Africa’s highest bridge—by hand.

Red Bull-sponsored thrill seeker, Thomas van Tonder, 34, and was born in South Africa took on 600 monkey bars that were fixed under the arch of the Bloukrans Bridge, en route to besting the longest set of bars ever built. And, as if this weren’t tough (or insane) enough, van Tonder had to follow the arch of the bridge, forcing him to to deal with an elevation and descent, all while his lactic acid was fit to burst.

At its peak, the bridge stood 216 meters above ground level, with van Tonder taking on 280 meters in distance. But on Oct. 26, 2026, the able athlete finished his perilous journey in 47 minutes and 37 seconds.

Van Tonder took on the most monkey bars, at the highest level, for the longest distance, but there were times when he questioned himself. “From the middle segment to the end, I was unsure if I’d actually make it,” he explained after he got firmly back on land.

To complete the challenge, van Tonder made strategic breaks by resting his legs on the bars, but this presented additional difficulties. “There were many points where I was on the edge of being able to actually get my legs up or not. It was definitely not a given.”

At the finish line, van Tonder was truly spent, and suffered with serious skin loss on his hands, but then making history was never easy. “One of the hardest things I’ve ever done,” he concluded.

Well, we’ll certainly never look at a set of monkey bars the same way again!

#8821. The Arizona Experiment!

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A big part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here.  It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,

“Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a new job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

Interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com

I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is currently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

As it stands, I have no plans beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a new phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

Looking forward to hearing about your time in AZ!

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.

#8818. Have Today’s Strength Machines Finally Caught Up with Free Weights for Muscle Growth?

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Since the invention of the barbell, free weights have long been considered the best for building muscle and strength. Machines? Those were for beginners, rehab, or finishing off a muscle after the real work.

Today, the barbell’s crown might be slipping.

Many well-equipped commercial gyms now have Pendulum squats, Arsenal Strength rows, converging chest presses, and other machines that look like they belong in a NASA training facility.

Modern designs feature sophisticated resistance curves and adjustable movement paths, letting lifters challenge their muscles without worrying about anything but the lift.

But before you put down the barbell, consider this question.

Are modern strength machines better for building muscle, or are we mistaking clever engineering for superior results?

They’re effective, versatile, and have helped generations of lifters build impressive muscle and strength.

“Free weights should always remain the foundation,” explains Matt Wenning of Wenning Strength. “They develop strength, coordination, and stability that machines cannot fully replicate.”

Here are three other reasons why they still work.

Barbells are easy to load, and most dumbbells increase in 2.5- to 5-pound increments. This makes it easy to track progress. Barbells let you handle heavier loads because they’re more stable than dumbbells.

Our bodies include prime mover muscles like the quads and smaller stabilizer muscles like the rotator cuff. Free weights engage both, but machines require less stabilization because they’re more stable. Stabilization helps build strength and coordination, but more stabilization doesn’t always mean more muscle.

Many machines have a fixed range of motion, but with dumbbells, you’re not locked into a fixed lifting path. This lets you adjust grip angles, elbow position, and pressing or pulling paths. That freedom lets you adjust to your needs and comfort.

Jay Ashman of Ashman Strength has a unique take on the rise of the machines.

“We are in the midst of the “optimization” trend, that’s heavy on aesthetics,” he explains. “Why would a trainee not use the easiest tool for the job? Doesn’t make it the best tool, but it’s the most efficient.”

Companies like Arsenal Strength, Rogers Athletic (Pendulum Strength), and Prime Fitness have taken advantage of that with more ways to customize exercises to your body.

A big development is how they apply resistance throughout an exercise’s range of motion. They do this with cams, lever arms, and adjustable loading positions. For example, some Prime Fitness machines offer multiple loading positions that let lifters emphasize different parts of the range of motion.

Why does this matter? Your muscles don’t produce equal force at every joint angle. A machine that places resistance where a muscle can produce more force may give you a muscle-building advantage.

Greater stability isn’t new, but it’s still worth mentioning. When you lift along a fixed path, without worrying about stabilizing, your target muscles get more love while your stabilizers take a break.

“If I’m trying to maximize mechanical tension through a particular muscle,” explains Gareth Sapstead, CSCS. “Reducing the stability demands can be a good thing because you’re challenging the target muscle rather than worrying about balance, coordination, or maintaining position.”

That’s handy when hypertrophy is the goal.

Adjustable Movement Paths and Better Ergonomics

The modern machines offer more ways to adjust your setup. Adjustable seats, chest pads, starting positions, handles, and range-of-motion settings help lifters find positions that better match their bodies. The newer chest press machines feature converging arms, allowing your hands to move closer together as you approach lockout. Some row machines use diverging movement paths, while others allow the arms to move independently.

Independent Loading and Unilateral Training

Another feature of many modern machines is independently moving arms.

Instead of both arms working together as a unit, each side moves separately. This lets lifters perform unilateral reps, notice side-to-side differences, and adjust their training if one side is weaker. Unilateral training isn’t new, but modern machines combine single-limb movement with stability and a guided path while reducing coordination demands.

Is one really better than the other for building strength and muscle? “We know that our muscles, “ explains Ashman. “We cannot tell the difference between free weights and machines regarding muscle growth.”

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis examined 13 studies involving 1,016 people comparing free-weight and machine training. Five of those studies measured hypertrophy, and the researchers found that neither had the advantage.

Another systematic review and meta-analysis by Heidel and colleagues concluded that machines and free weights both built similar amounts of muscle. A separate 2023 study comparing free-weight and machine-based exercises found similar improvements in muscle hypertrophy and strength between training approaches.

NOTE: These studies compare general categories of machines and free weights, not the newest machines featuring adjustable resistance profiles.

Although muscle growth appears the same, the strength findings reveal something interesting.

The Haugen meta-analysis found that lifters who trained with free weights improved more when tested with free weights. Those who trained with machines also performed better on machine-based strength tests. Strength is equipment-specific, with limited crossover in technique. For example, a Pendulum squat develops the quads and glutes, but it won’t teach the same balance, coordination, or barbell-specific technique as a barbell back squat.

You’ve seen that science can’t separate them. But with all the money they’ve poured into development, they must have the muscle-building edge.

Let’s compare the Pendulum Squat to the barbell squat to see where the modern machine might offer an advantage.

The Pendulum squat uses a guided, arcing motion that reduces balance demands. Depending on the machine’s design and your setup, this can make it easier to achieve depth and focus on leg drive. Some Pendulum machines also feature resistance profiles that adjust how challenging different portions of the movement feel.

The Machine advantage: Greater external stability allows some lifters to challenge their quads more without balance, bar positioning, or torso control becoming the limiting factor. For lifters with mobility limitations or discomfort supporting a barbell, the Pendulum Squat machine offers a viable alternative.

The barbell advantage: The back squat develops barbell-specific strength, coordination, and the ability to control heavy loads. It’s also essential for competitive powerlifters and more versatile for developing lower-body strength.

The verdict: If your goal is bigger quads, the Pendulum squat may be a better fit, but it doesn’t guarantee greater muscle growth. For more total-body strength and muscle, the barbell is still your best bet.

Modern machines let you focus on specific muscles and ranges of motion, and you can adjust the setup to suit your needs, but strength training is more than just building muscle.

Maximal Strength and Exercise Specificity

If your goal is to improve maximal strength, the barbell is still the way to go. No amount of Pendulum squats will fully replace the skill, coordination, and technique required to get under a heavy bar and squat. Barbell squats also improve your ability to coordinate muscle actions, stabilize the load, and produce force in that movement.

Machines can strengthen the muscles involved, but they don’t reproduce every demand of a free-weight lift.

Free weights require you to control the load rather than allowing the machine to guide it. This means coordinating multiple joints, maintaining your position, and adjusting your movement as the weight travels through space.

“I still favor free weights for developing strength, coordination, positional control,” explains Sapstead. “The ability to produce force through more complex movement patterns works well for clients who want a physique that performs as well as it looks.”

Modern machines reduce some of those demands, but free weights offer a better chance to practice coordination and movement skills under load.

With free weights, you have everything you need for a great workout. They make it easy to modify exercises without changing equipment. Adjust your grip, stance, range of motion, or body position to change the training stimulus.

Modern machines, especially premium plate-loaded equipment, cost more, take up more space, and often serve a specific purpose.

Modern machines have challenged the idea that barbells and dumbbells are superior for building muscle, but free weights are popular for a reason. Free weights remain essential for developing specific strength, offer greater versatility, and demand movements that many machines reduce.

“Free weights have an important place, and I wouldn’t necessarily say one is better than the other,” says Sapstead.

The question isn’t whether machines have dethroned free weights. It’s whether you’re choosing the right equipment for your goals. For most lifters, the answer is both, not either or.

Sapstead’s approach is refreshing. “The best exercise is the one that places sufficient tension on the muscles you’re trying to develop through a useful range of motion while allowing consistent progression,” he says.

“Sometimes that’s a barbell, sometimes a dumbbell, and sometimes a really well-designed machine.”

There’s no need to pick a side, but you do need to choose exercises based on the three factors below.

If your goal is a bigger squat, deadlift, or bench, free weights rule because you need to be under or over the barbell. “Machines should support your free-weight training, not replace it, “ says Wenning.

But building muscle offers you more flexibility between free weights and machines. The important question isn’t whether you use a machine or free weights to build muscle. It’s all about progressive overload. If one is easier for you, go with it.

Use Machines to Reduce Unnecessary Fatigue

Modern machines let you adjust your setup for enhanced stability, so you don’t have to worry about stabilizing or balancing. This doesn’t mean machines eliminate fatigue or that free weights always produce more. It means that choosing exercises with different stability and positioning demands can help distribute fatigue more effectively throughout your workout. Wenning agrees.

“Machines are tools to help improve performance with free weights,” he explains. “They allow us to isolate weaknesses, build additional muscle, and increase training volume without the same level of systemic fatigue.”

Pushing the limits with free weights often requires a spotter. If you want to do a bench-press drop set and you don’t have a spotter, wouldn’t it be better and more efficient to do it on a chest-press machine, where failure doesn’t mean you’re pinned under the barbell?

Sapstead agrees. “ Taking a hack squat or leg extension to failure is generally more manageable than doing the same with a heavy barbell squat.”

So does Ashman. “Training to failure is much safer on a machine than with free weights, and because I’m seeing an emphasis on “effective reps” and training close to failure.”

This workout combines free-weight pressing with supported machine pulling.

This lower-body workout combines free-weight hip-hinge and unilateral exercises with machine-based training.

Now more than ever, machines are neck and neck with free weights in the muscle-building stakes.

With improved resistance profiles, greater stability, and more adjustable lifting paths, today’s machines have earned their place alongside barbells and dumbbells in the weight room.

But have they overtaken free weights for building muscle? Not quite.

Research shows that machines and free weights can produce similar muscle growth, and we don’t yet have convincing evidence that newer machines yield superior results.

But it is not about choosing sides; it’s about choosing which better fits your goals and body type.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins

Here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

Virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart currently prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:

For a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

Virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

Do NOT start at Virgin Atlantic's website — their search tool for partner awards is limited. Instead, go directly to delta.com and search for your desired route (e.g., JFK → LAX) in the date range you're targeting. Select "Use miles" as your payment method and filter by Business class. You're not booking here — you're prospecting.

What you're looking for: Delta One availability showing in the results. When you see it, note the exact flight number, date, and departure time. Delta.com will show you the SkyMiles price (which will be high under dynamic pricing), but ignore that number entirely. You just need to confirm the seat exists.

You need 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person. Before transferring anything, confirm which flexible points currency you're working with:

All transfer at 1:1 instantly. If you're using Marriott Bonvoy points, the ratio is 3:1 (so 150,000 Bonvoy points = 50,000 Flying Club miles), and transfers take 1–5 days.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific flight, transfer your points. Use the transfer portal within your credit card program's website (Chase, Amex, Citi, or Bilt). You'll need your Flying Club membership number — create a free account at virginatlantic.com/us/en/flying-club if you don't have one.

For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers: miles appear instantly in your Flying Club account. Confirm the balance before proceeding.

Critical warning: Do not transfer points until you've verbally confirmed availability with a Virgin Atlantic agent (Step 4). Points transfers are irreversible.

This is a phone booking, not an online booking. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at 1-800-365-9500. Have your flight details ready:

Ask the agent to confirm that Delta One award availability exists on your chosen flight before you transfer points. If they confirm it, then transfer and call back — or ask to be placed on a brief hold while you complete the transfer (instant transfers make this possible).

Once your miles are transferred and the agent has confirmed availability, they'll complete the booking. You'll pay only standard carrier taxes and fees — expect roughly $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. route. You'll receive a Virgin Atlantic booking confirmation, but your ticket will show Delta as the operating carrier.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. For the best seat selection and availability, aim to search within that window as early as possible.

Delta SkyMiles uses fully dynamic pricing with no published award chart, meaning business class awards can range from 80,000 to 500,000 SkyMiles for the same route depending on demand. Virgin Atlantic, as a Delta joint venture partner, maintains a fixed award chart for Delta-operated flights — creating a massive pricing arbitrage. A JFK-to-London Delta One Suite that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles can often be booked through Virgin for 47,500 Flying Club miles. Both programs see the same award inventory, but Virgin prices it using their distance-based chart instead of Delta's demand-based algorithm. Since Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club accepts 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, you can earn these miles through credit card spending without ever flying Virgin Atlantic.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers become concrete.

The Route: New York JFK → Los Angeles LAX The Aircraft: Airbus A350-900 The Cabin: Delta One Suites

Pull up Delta.com on a typical travel date and you'll find Delta One Suites on this route priced anywhere from $2,500 for a off-peak weekday to $5,000–$6,000 during peak summer weekends or holiday travel. Let's use a realistic midpoint of $3,500 — a completely standard price for business class on one of America's most competitive routes.

If you earned those 50,000 points via a Chase Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus (currently 60,000 points) and some organic spend, your real cost to acquire the points was a small fraction of the flight's retail value.

You check in at JFK's Terminal 4 with Delta status access or a Priority Pass card in hand, clearing into the Delta Sky Club or the premium Centurion Lounge (if you carry the Amex Platinum). Then you board the A350-900 and find your suite.

The five-hour flight from New York to Los Angeles becomes an experience rather than a commute. You arrive rested, full, and having spent roughly $11 out of pocket on a seat your fellow passengers paid $3,500 for. That gap — that's the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in action.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. Delta One availability on high-demand routes like JFK–LAX is not unlimited — it's released in waves and often fills quickly for peak dates. Set a calendar reminder to search exactly 331 days before your target travel date. This is especially important for holiday travel, summer weekends, and any dates where you have a hard deadline.

Since transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are instant, you can do a same-call transfer — confirm availability with the agent, ask them to hold for a moment, transfer your points in a separate browser tab, and confirm with the agent that the miles have landed. This eliminates the risk of availability disappearing between your transfer and your booking attempt.

While this sweet spot is available year-round, Delta One availability is generally better on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday departures when leisure demand is lower. If your travel dates are flexible, searching across a week of dates will often surface better availability on midweek flights.

Virgin Atlantic's award chart has high fuel surcharges on Virgin Atlantic-operated flights. This guide is specifically about Delta-operated flights. Never confuse the two. When you call to book, confirm the operating carrier is Delta. The surcharge-free benefit applies only to partner awards.

Points transfers are irreversible. A common and painful mistake is transferring points to Flying Club only to discover the specific flight you wanted has no award availability. Always confirm availability verbally with a Flying Club agent before initiating any transfer.

The most efficient path to 50,000 points is a single credit card welcome bonus. The Chase Sapphire Preferred or Chase Sapphire Reserve both offer welcome bonuses that can fully fund this redemption — and both transfer to Virgin Atlantic at 1:1 instantly. Alternatively, the Amex Gold Card or Platinum Card welcome bonuses work equally well via Amex's instant transfer path.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A simple fix: make a small earning transaction (even a hotel stay or car rental through their partners) at least once every three years.

Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at their US number. Provide the specific flight number, date, and route you found on delta.com. The agent will search for the same availability and quote the mileage cost from Virgin's fixed award chart. Confirm the booking and pay taxes and fees.

Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart prices Delta One flights based on distance. Transatlantic routes (US to Europe) typically cost 47,500 to 60,000 Virgin miles one-way in business class. Transpacific routes cost more, around 60,000 to 80,000 miles. Compare this to Delta SkyMiles, which can charge 200,000 to 500,000 miles for the same seats.

#8809. Stanford AI May Have Discovered a Natural Ozempic Alternative for Weight Loss

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

With a monthly course of the synthetic weight loss drug, Ozempic costing upward of $1,000 per month without insurance, news that researchers at Stanford harnessed AI to locate a natural compound that could lead to new drugs is welcome news. But what exactly what is this molecule, and how did AI help to identify it?

The discovery of the organic compound was first unveiled as the results of a March 2025 study, which looked at peptide hormones and the effects on energy regulation. During the study, experts programmed AI to map peptide fragments and found that a 12-amino-acid molecule, labeled “BRP” acted in a distinct, but similar way to semaglutide, potentially offering an even more targeted approach to dropping fat.

“The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues,” explained Katrin Svensson, PhD, who is an assistant professor of pathology at Stanford, and was the lead author of the breakthrough study. “That’s why Ozempic has widespread effects, including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism.”

AI drastically accelerated the identification of BRP thanks to it’s superior processing power, because traditional methods of protein isolation face difficulties with distinguishing peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) from the more prevalent  natural byproducts of protein degradation and processing. The researchers had designed a new algorithm that inspected 20,000 protein-coding genes, narrowing the field down to 373 prohormones containing 2,683 peptides. The team then focused on peptide sequences that were likely to be bioactive in the brain, just like GLP-1 drugs, and screened 100 such peptides.

When the researchers put BRP to the test on lean mice and miniature pigs (which more closely mirror human eating and digestion than mice), they discovered that an intramuscular injection of BRP, prior to feeding, reduced food intake over the next hour by up to 50% in both animal models, meaning that with less energy consumed, fat levels would decrease with repeat treatments. Further studies of physiological and brain activity illustrated that BRP activates metabolic and neuronal pathways in these animals that are different from those activated by GLP-1 or semaglutide.

Following the study’s promising results, Svensson soon co-founded a company to launch clinical trials of the molecule. But before it can be released to humans, further work is now underway to investigating how to help BRP’s effects last longer, to allow a more convenient dosing schedule, should this peptide prove to be effective in regulating human body weight.

BRP’s results on humans is yet to be published, but while there is no firm date for its release confirmed as of now, the synergy between human scientists and AI could prove to be a gamechanger. While Ozempic is a synthetic medication, the discovery of more natural molecules like BRP could provide a more natural, and potentially cheaper approach.

“The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades,” said Svensson. “Nothing we’ve tested before has compared to semaglutide’s ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if (BRP) is safe and effective in humans.”

#8805. This Year’s NYC Marathon Proved Different Strategies Can Lead to Victory

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

I’m sure I could think of a couple of thousand ways, many of which include espresso, to spend a Sunday morning in New York City than running 26.2 miles through all five boroughs. But on Nov. 1, nearly 60,000 people decided to run the New York City Marathon—again—like they have every year since 1970. Some were chasing a championship. Some were chasing a personal best. Others probably just wanted to finish before their feet decided to go on strike. And there are hosts of runners dressed in all kinds of costumes just out for a jog. And the crowd keeps everyone well cheered on. No matter who it is.

The men’s winner was Andreas Almgren of Sweden, who covered the course in two hours, six minutes, one second. And I’m going to put an asterisk next to it because this was his first marathon. Not his first race, obviously. Almgren arrived as the reigning world half-marathon champion and European 10,000-meter champion. He’d spent years developing the engine. He just hadn’t taken it out for this particular 26.2-mile test drive.

The lead pack stayed together deep into the race, and Almgren waited until the final mile to make his decisive move. Italy’s Yemaneberhan Crippa finished second, thirteen seconds behind him, and Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third. Defending champion Benson Kipruto wound up fourth. That’s quite a debut, particularly on a course that includes bridges, hills, crazy potholes and enough turns to get you lost.

Before anybody decides the lesson is to skip marathon preparation, understand what a debut means here. Almgren wasn’t some guy who woke up last Thursday and discovered running shoes. He had world-class credentials at shorter distances. Moving up required applying an already extraordinary aerobic foundation to a longer event. A marathon is not merely two half-marathons stapled together. Fueling, pacing, muscular endurance, and how you respond after mile twenty all become rather important when your body starts negotiating terms of surrender.

The women’s race was even more entertaining near the finish. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui reclaimed the title she’d won in 2024, finishing in 2:24:36. Defending champion Hellen Obiri was in the fight late, but American Jess McClain came charging from behind and passed her in the closing meters. Chepkirui won, McClain took second in 2:24:42, and Obiri was third one second later. McClain became the first American woman on the New York podium since 2018.

And if you think the only interesting athletes are the ones with the smallest numbers on the clock, the wheelchair divisions cranks them out! Switzerland’s Marcel Hug won his eighth New York title in 1:28:14, edging American Daniel Romanchuk by one second. Catherine Debrunner, also Swiss, won the women’s wheelchair race in 1:40:02, nearly eight and a half minutes ahead of Tatyana McFadden. Same city, same event, completely different demands on the athlete. The upper-body power, equipment handling, and tactical judgment involved deserve more attention than they usually get.

Then there’s Mildred Baker, an 80-year-old Bronx resident who took up running in her late seventies and completed her first marathon in 7:03:49. Seven freakin’ hours! No, Almgren is not the only champion. That’s the point. The marathon can be a world championship-level knife fight at the front and a personal expedition at the back. And a trade in between. You can appreciate both extremes without pretending they’re the same athletic achievement.

Secondly, I must admit that l like the way this race exposes a certain kind of gym stupidity: the assumption that only one type of physical performance counts. A Swedish speed merchant conquered a distance he’d never raced. An American woman stole second place in the final strides. An 80-year-old finished something most people wouldn’t even start. You’re actually, in one Sunday event, looking at the entire definition of fitness.
