“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.

Run that $45,000 annual gap through 25 years at a 5% real return and it grows to about $2.15 million by age 60, a fortune separating two doctors with the same income at the same hospital, parked in the same doctors’ lot, one of them driving home to a plan and the other to a calculator that reads like a death certificate.

Addams spent every productivity bonus. You’ve already met her at 11 PM.

You go from a resident making $65,000 to an attending earning $350,000, and the word “deserve” moves into your vocabulary. A bigger house. Then tens of thousands sunk into renovating it, followed by the new car, the au pair, private school, and first class to Maui.

Nobody warns you how hard it is to downshift once you’ve gotten used to the view. Your brain resets “normal” to match your paycheck and refuses to reset it back, so the spending tags along into retirement like a party guest who showed up uninvited and also brought luggage.

I watched an Arizona cardiologist discover at 66 that he needed $400,000 a year to keep living the way he lived. His portfolio could safely throw off maybe $180,000. He’s 71 now. Still full-time.

Simple, boring solution: live like a resident for two to five years after training, bank the gap, kill the student loans, and upgrade slowly enough that your brain never registers the drift.

Nearly every physician gets pitched whole life insurance, usually by a friend or relative whose licensing exam ink is still wet. The illustration promises cash value, tax-free growth, and a death benefit, all in one tidy package.

For most physicians who need life insurance, it’s mostly garbage. Premiums run many times higher than term. Commissions feed on the early years, and the cash value grows like it’s been bled.

Run an illustrative comparison: one physician pays $3,000 a month into whole life, while her colleague buys 20-year term for around $150 a month and invests the other $2,850, and at a 7% return that side account sits near $1.5 million after 20 years, with the policy’s cash value usually trailing by hundreds of thousands, still waiting for the illustration to come true.

Sold by family, illustrated in optimistic colors, and funded for 15 years by a doctor too busy to read past page two, Dr. Addams’s three policies carried combined premiums of $8,400 a month and a total cash value of $780,000.

Term plus investing would likely have left her near $1.9 million. She surrendered all three at 58. Ate the surrender charges. Started catching up.

In plenty of physician households, one person earns the money and the same person manages it.

Then the doctor dies, divorces, or has a stroke at 63, and the spouse inherits decades of decisions made behind a closed door, written in a language nobody bothered to teach them.

I’ve sat with widows who found out their physician husband had:

A spouse at the table pulls decisions toward the conservative side, a handy counterweight when the 2 AM version of you thinks genius has struck.

Build the plan simple enough that they could run it alone. Keep the account list and passwords somewhere they can actually find, which rules out your head.

Business school professors have a phrase for the bad investments that circulate in medical circles: deals that can only be sold to doctors.

Time poverty and overconfidence do the damage. Researching an investment takes hours you don’t have, so you trust people, and you assume that mastering the coagulation cascade somehow qualifies you to underwrite private equity. It doesn’t.

Physicians I know have poured money into restaurant groups that folded within 18 months, real estate “opportunities” that smelled faintly of Ponzi, and crypto tokens launched by a nephew’s roommate’s brother.

Index funds are boring. They work. Put $50,000 a year into low-cost index funds for 30 years at a 5% real return and you end up with about $3.32 million.

Lose 2% a year to fees and the same contributions grow to about $2.38 million, close to a million dollars handed to people in nicer suits than yours. If your portfolio needs a 40-page binder to explain, you’re the mark.

Most physicians blow past the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December, which puts you among the few groups who routinely qualify for the maximum benefit. Claiming age is a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month. Wait until full retirement age and that rises to $4,152. Hold out to 70 and it’s roughly $5,181.

Dr. Lucky filed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums at $200 an hour, and because Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 before full retirement age, his own paycheck ate his benefit, which the SSA hands back after full retirement age in small monthly crumbs.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a premium no insurer will match. A serious diagnosis can justify claiming early.

For a healthy 62-year-old with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call. You’ve delivered enough prognoses to know which patient you are.

Most physicians stuff nearly everything into pre-tax accounts during peak years, which makes sense at 37%. Trouble arrives when that’s the only move for 25 years, because a $4 million pre-tax portfolio is a smaller number dressed up for the party.

If you need $180,000 a year to live and pull it entirely from pre-tax accounts, you might withdraw $240,000 to get there. Your 4.5% withdrawal plan just became a 6% plan.

Required minimum distributions start at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security. Then Medicare notices.

IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Thanks for this informative and entertaining article. should be required reading for all docs. Made me realize that I am fortunate to have avoided the worst of bad decisions. I’m 78 now and comfortably retired with close family. Life is good.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. We have written an article on retirement that might compliment the informative blog here. Whereas it is focused on academic physicians, there are many points applicable to those in practice (Greenberg L, Fischel JE, Siegel B. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

They left out the annuity with a 5% rate guaranteed growth with step ups if the market does better than 5% minus fees. You can attach an ins package for your spouse. take a 4% W/D on your money. dont increase your standard of living to just be like everyone else. avoid the race to nowhere and stay away from out of state tuition. your kids will do well anywhere they go if they apply themselves: they got the intellect and drive from their parents not private school or private universities. Cars get you to and from work – where is the luxury? in the car dealerships pocket. Bigger houses dont mean happy homes and what do you do with the extra bedrooms when the adults start their own lives? Money left over after you max a 401k with a profit sharing plan (employ your spouse after the kids are gone), time to put extra into index funds with a downside sharing of risk. might not make the 14-19% that other are making but none of the panic when covid 2.0 comes to the shore. I went through 3 financial planners (all with vacation homes on my money) before I found Andrew. I was sold when he asked me a simple question. How much do you spend per month? Let’s see how much you have to have saved to make that per year with inflation. Its amazing how much you can love medicine when you can retire whenever the fancy hits you once you have attained the above goal!

Thanks for sharing your journey! You’ve clearly learned the hard lessons that most physicians skip—keeping lifestyle inflation in check, avoiding the luxury trap, and finding a real fiduciary advisor after getting burned by commission-chasing “planners” (those vacation homes weren’t free!).

Your point about annuities is worth noting for the right situation, though they’re not for everyone. The real gold in your comment is this: “How much do you spend per month?” Most physicians never ask themselves this question until it’s too late. They assume their income means they’re wealthy, then discover their spending ate everything.

The freedom you describe—loving medicine because you can retire whenever you want—that’s what happens when you get the math right early. You avoided the nightmare by doing exactly what Dr. Addams eventually learned: live below your means, ignore the Joneses, and make the boring financial moves that actually work.

This was an informative and entertaining article: creatively written with the Halloween metaphors!

#8711. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!)

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.)

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out.  I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:24 am

I read that many of the people in that (wealthy) part of LA were forced to self-insure partly because the insurance companies weren’t willing to cover such a high wildfire risk. At a certain level of wealth, the cost of repairing or rebuilding a house isn’t a big deal but I’m sure there are many people left behind and struggling.

For the rest of us, it’s really just a probability game: if you can’t afford the consequences of a fire or disaster, either buy insurance or stick to a less expensive house. If you ARE getting insurance, do the math on whether the premium is worth the coverage.

Homeowners also includes liability protection if someone is injured on your property and for certain off-property related claims, like if you injure someone with your bicycle, or get sued for slander or libel. Also it generally would be required before one could have an umbrella policy for higher liability coverage. Maybe this is more of a U.S. mindset, than an Canadian one where there are fewer outlandish personal injury judgments, but for me having insurance to protect my net worth is an important consideration. So I carry la homeowner’s policy for asset protection.

This is a very good point. I am a retired insurance regulatory lawyer, and homeowners insurance just covers much more than the house. It covers YOU for liability. If you get sued, it also hires a lawyer to defend you and pays any judgement against you up to the policy limits. It also provides loss of use coverage to pay for the hotel you have to live in if your house becomes uninhabitable AND pays to replace the contents of your house, like your furniture, appliances, and clothes.

You write that, “Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.”

You don’t have home insurance?!?! Say if your house burns down? Isn’t it worth it to have insurance to cover that catastrophic loss? I pay a small amount monthly for this benefit. Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:21 am

Yes, for many people house insurance is a solid plan. And if you have a mortgage on that house, it’s mandatory because the lender wants YOU to pay to protect THEIR collateral.

As you get older and wealthier, and especially if you live in a not-that-expensive house like my current one, it’s worth it to continually rework the math. In my case I came up with these thoughts:

– if my house burned down, I’d be rather pissed but the actual cost of rebuilding would not affect my ability to stay retired – and the foundation would probably survive, which cuts the rebuilding costs by another $50k or so – and I’d rebuild it into a much cooler house – and I’d be the builder and hire all my carpenter friends to work alongside me, because that’s my favorite thing to do anyway!

Another factor is just the “sleep at night” question. If having insurance helps you sleep better at night, that increases the value for you as well. In my case, I sleep like a worry-free log every night anyway :-)

What I’ve come to realize is that when you really dig down to a meaningful life, you don’t actually *need* to always be striving for something different from what you already have.

I mean yes, I generally try to be helpful in the ways that I can, both locally and on a bigger scale with things like sharing ideas on the internet. But there’s an (ADHD-informed) balance where I need a certain amount of free time and I work best in an unscheduled life where I only decide what to do most days AFTER a good morning walk and breakfast.

Single mom with a teen living in an expensive city (I know…) so no FIRE for me yet, but your posts have kept me on a frugal path for more than a decade, so I thank you. Having a paid-off house with very low costs (solar powered, do a lot of my own repairs) and a rental property I will get there much sooner than I previously thought possible.

This is a great question and conversation starter. I retired early about two years ago, and I’m early in the process of considering these big ideas. I think a lot about how to do the most I can for my community without turning over 100% of my time to somebody else’s goals and whims.

A couple of core principles that I’m drawn to:

1. It’s all about the 80/20 rule — what are the 20% of actions we can take that will make 80% of the change? Pick one thing that aligns with your skills, interests, and influence, and work on that. For MMM, it’s reducing car traffic (and thereby carbon emissions) by persuading people to design their lives around biking. For me, it’s increasing literacy, particularly media literacy. I think if Americans were better able to distinguish propaganda, scams, etc. from good information, we would be much more effective at creating policies that benefit as many people as possible.

2. Giving money can be just as good (or better!!) than giving your time. I completely get MMM’s point here that it’s counterproductive to be locked into running a nonprofit full-time if that’s not how you work best. I believe people who prefer more time freedom can feel great about “just” providing funding for others who find meaning in devoting a lot of time to hands-on work. (And many people, like me, will fall in the middle, with some part-time volunteering and some donating.)

Many of us worry about problems that we have no real expertise in or direct control over, like preventing wildfires. It is a huge contribution to donate money strategically to the people who do have the expertise and the control, even if your time is going only to making art, enjoying nature, hanging out with friends, etc. We learned from MMM that our money works harder than us, and that can apply to charitable giving too!

I’ve benefited from the EV tax credit, but at the same time I don’t like the federal government distorting the market, but then also at the same time the federal government already does that in so many areas with ridiculous Byzantine regulations, so the EV tax credit could be seen as a form of “un-distortion”. Either way, if the tax credit disappears I am quite confident that the market will find a new equilibrium all on its own.

I’ve heard that “subsidy/distorted market” argument about EVs so many times over the past few years, and yet I find it mostly irrelevant. I think most people don’t know that the combustion engine vehicles industry has been heavily subsidized for decades, either through tax breaks, direct investments from the government, direct subsidies to oil companies and, in a more subtle way, by very lax environmental regulations that have allowed the production of these vehicles (or oil) at a distorted cost. The only difference is that when buying EVs, consumers receive the tax credit directly instead of getting a hidden discount on a combustion engine vehicle that was subsidized on the production line. It is a “subsidy” in the sense that it reduces monthly/yearly cash requirements by the amount of principal+interest (and in the case of MMM, insurance since he chooses to self-insure). If you have a mortgage then you have a requirement to pay the mortgage every month (PITI), but in MMM’s case he only pays the ‘T’ part or taxes.

If he had a mortgage, then his $30k/year spend would probably be closer to $60k/year (or something, depending on the amount financed, interest rates, insurance, etc.). So the subsidy is the reduction in annual spending because of not having the mortgage. But he got that by working at paying off the mortgage earlier in life, which he acknowledges is a trade off.

It sounds like you had a bunch of fun and got to spend “tons” of money without impacting your long term finances, and instead continuing to let them grow.

#8707. Black Friday TVs & Laptops Can Be Stripped-Down Versions – Check the Model Number

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Some Black Friday TVs and laptops are cheaper versions built for the sale, and on a store page they look almost identical to the regular model reviewers tested. Before you buy a doorbuster, look up its full model number on the brand’s site and compare its specs with the regular model’s.

Consumer Reports calls these TVs derivatives, since they’re derived from a brand’s regular models. Some are sold by only one retailer, so there’s no other store’s price to compare.

Two 65-inch TVs from one brand can have model numbers a character or two apart, yet one has a 120Hz refresh rate, meaning it redraws the picture 120 times a second, and the other 60Hz. The faster screen shows sports and video games more smoothly.

A derivative can have fewer HDMI ports, the inputs for a game console or soundbar, and the reviews you find may cover only the regular model. Laptops work the same way, since one model name can cover several versions, and the one on sale can have a slower processor or less storage than the one reviewers tested.

Then look up the item’s price history, which shows whether the sale price is actually low.

Consumer Reports brings some derivatives into its lab and often finds major-brand ones that perform as well as regular models priced $100 to $150 higher. So a derivative is a sound buy when its specs match how you’ll use it, such as a 60Hz set with two HDMI ports in a guest room that only streams shows.

My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.

Nothing in residency prepared me for the cadaver head course. Severed heads rested face up in disposable roasting pans, lined down a row of tables, while surgeons calmly rehearsed facelifts. I kept my coffee down, though it was close.

Consider the advantages. These patients won’t ask about downtime or bring up a cousin’s botched eyelid job, and the state board will hear nothing from them. Somebody should study their satisfaction scores.

Medicine has always practiced on the dead, and for a long stretch it practiced on dead people who never agreed to the arrangement.

Nineteenth-century anatomy schools bought corpses from grave robbers and asked few questions about provenance. In Edinburgh in 1828, William Burke and William Hare decided digging was too slow, murdered sixteen people, and sold the bodies to anatomist Robert Knox.

Britain answered with the Anatomy Act of 1832, which handed medical schools the unclaimed bodies of the poor. Reform, of a sort.

Physicians have spent centuries trying to pin down the second a person stops being a person. We have never once nailed it.

In 1905, a French doctor named Beaurieux stood beside the guillotine as a convict named Languille lost his head. Beaurieux called out the man’s name. By his own report, the eyelids lifted and the eyes fixed on him before closing, and the trick worked a second time before it quit for good.

Consciousness or reflex? Nobody could say then, and we can’t now.

Cleveland, 1970. Neurosurgeon Robert White transplanted the head of one rhesus monkey onto the body of another, and the head woke up and tracked people around the room. White spent the rest of his career insisting the operation could work in humans.

I met my own version of this riddle at the bedside of a brain-dead organ donor. He was warm and pink. His heart pumped, his kidneys made urine, and at one point a spinal reflex lifted his arm off the sheet, the move clinicians call the Lazarus sign.

The nurse beside me didn’t flinch. I did. Legally he had died hours earlier, and the procurement team was already en route.

Hospice taught me the rest. Dying unfolds over hours or days, a slow dimming no monitor captures cleanly, yet the death certificate demands a single timestamp. So we pick one and move on.

For several centuries, European apothecaries sold ground-up mummy as medicine. Physicians prescribed it for bruises, bleeding and a long menu of complaints, and when genuine Egyptian stock ran short, enterprising suppliers manufactured fresh “mummy” from whatever bodies they could find.

Folklore adds “mellified man,” a corpse supposedly steeped in honey for a century and sold by the chunk. Historians doubt he ever existed. I’ve seen supplement labels make bolder claims.

The dead, for all their weirdness, behave predictably. They stay where you put them. The living refuse that courtesy.

Beginning in the early 2000s, hundreds of children in Sweden withdrew into a state that looked like coma. Nearly all came from asylum-seeking families facing deportation.

They quit eating and talking, then quit opening their eyes, and some stayed that way for a year or longer while parents turned them in bed and nurses ran their feeding tubes. Swedish doctors named it uppgivenhetssyndrom. Resignation syndrome.

Scans came back clean, and so did the labs. Nobody found a virus, a toxin or a lesion. The condition clustered almost entirely inside Swedish borders, and many of the children surfaced slowly once their families won permission to stay.

That makes a lot of physicians squirm. The suffering is real, the paralysis is real, and the driver is a mind expressing despair in the shape its surroundings taught it to take.

I’ve watched a milder version play out in hospice more times than I can count. A patient holds steady for weeks, the family meeting goes sideways, and by the next morning he has stopped eating.

In the Kazakh village of Kalachi, starting around 2013, residents began dozing off mid-sentence. Some slept for days and woke with no memory of it. A shuttered Soviet uranium mine sat down the road, which made for a tidy villain.

Officials tested the air, water and soil, and the government eventually relocated much of the town. Plenty of clinicians point instead to a community watching its jobs and young people drain away, taking any sense of a future with them.

Le Roy, New York, ran a similar script in 2011. A cluster of high school girls developed tics, jerks and verbal outbursts that spread through the school and lit up the evening news.

Erin Brockovich showed up to investigate a chemical spill from a 1970 train derailment. Neurologists diagnosed conversion disorder, a label the families received with roughly the enthusiasm you’d expect.

I’ve delivered that diagnosis myself. The MRI was perfect, the legs still wouldn’t move, and the patient heard “it’s all in your head” no matter how carefully I phrased it. She left to find a doctor who would order another scan.

A toxin is a gift, because it blames no one. A functional diagnosis blames no one either, yet patients hear an accusation in it, and plenty of us deliver it like one. We fumble that conversation more often than we fumble a central line.

Among the Miskito people on Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast, young women fall prey to grisi siknis. They collapse, then bolt into the night, and later describe a dark stranger who came to carry them off.

Village healers treat it with rituals and herbs, and it hops from one community to the next like a bad cold.

Wealthy countries have their own spirits. In El Carmen de Bolívar, Colombia, in 2014, schoolgirls began fainting and convulsing after HPV vaccination. Videos of their episodes ricocheted across social media, and the country’s HPV vaccination rate collapsed.

Two years later, American diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and strange sounds, and the press settled on a mysterious energy weapon. Some neurologists argue for a more mundane explanation that nobody in Washington wanted to hear.

Our culture supplies the toxins, the radio waves and the MRI that might at last catch the culprit. The Miskito get a dark stranger, while our demons come with CPT codes.

Funerals are where the haunted house collides with your financial plan. The National Funeral Directors Association put the 2023 median cost of a funeral with viewing and burial at about $8,300, and a funeral with cremation at roughly $6,280. Your aunt’s flower budget comes extra.

Whole-body donation to a medical school typically covers transport and cremation and returns the ashes to family, often at little or no cost. Programs vary, so call the school before you count on it.

Your body could spend its retirement crash-testing airbags or showing some nervous first-year where the brachial plexus hides. Mine would be in good company. I still owe that woman with the coral nail polish.

Physicians spend years making sure the 401(k) has a beneficiary. Few of us spend ten minutes deciding who gets the rest of the estate, meaning the part with the liver in it. Put it in writing this Halloween, somewhere between the will and the trust, and let your remains keep earning after you clock out.

I’d always assumed harvesting was something you did in a crash. Turns out the losses are there every year, buried inside individual lots, waiting for someone to notice.

A lunch bought at work averages about $14, while one you pack costs about $4 to $5 in groceries. At those prices, packing four days a week saves well over $1,000 a year. Cook extra at dinner so tomorrow’s lunch is already made, and plan one lunch out a week to make the habit last.

Buying lunch rarely feels expensive because you pay for it one meal at a time. The Fooda Price Index, built from millions of sales at pop-up restaurants inside workplaces, puts that meal at $13.90 on average.

Run your own numbers before you start. Subtract what a packed lunch costs from what you usually pay for a bought one, then multiply by the lunches you’d pack in a year. The USDA’s moderate-cost food plan, a grocery budget for healthy meals made at home, allows $76.50 to $91.90 a week for an adult aged 20 to 70 in a four-person household. Spread over a week’s 21 meals, that’s about $4 each. For someone who lives alone, the USDA suggests adding 20%, which puts a meal closer to $5.

Say you work 48 weeks a year and pack four days a week. Swapping a $14 bought lunch for a $4 packed one saves $10 a lunch, or $1,920 over 192 lunches a year.

Packing doesn’t have to mean cooking a second time each day. Three habits make it quick:

A lunch out you’ve planned makes the other four days easier to pack. Pick the day now, such as Friday with coworkers, and put it on your calendar.

Can you count on Social Security in retirement? While the retirement trust fund is projected to run out in 2032, according to the 2026 Trustees Report, benefits will still be paid out, just at a lower percentage. How much lower? 78% of scheduled benefits. That’s a 22% reduction, which is real. But it’s not a 100% reduction!

On average, heirs typically receive inherited IRAs at age 59, and the mean balance of those accounts is $128,000, according to a recent Vanguard report. Those accounts can be a sizable windfall, but taxes could take a chunk without proper planning, experts say. Original account owners may consider Roth conversions, strategic beneficiaries moves and other tactics.

When it comes to investing, people fixate on the risks of the stock market: What if the market crashes? Will I get the return I expected? How much can I draw down from investments each year without running out of money? Those are all valid concerns. But they are far from the only risks out there. What’s more, if you spend too much time focusing on just one risk then you are liable to make poor decisions.

The SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs are every money lesson in miniature: There’s the gap between the number on the screen and the money you can actually spend, the tax bill that stalks you home from the party, the way a big, sudden pile of money makes smart people stop thinking clearly. You don’t need stock options to learn any of that. You just need to see it laid out simply enough that the shame falls away.

Finding bliss is centered around not looking for it. Pursuing feelings is a road to nowhere. Fixating on yourself is a recipe for an unsatisfactory life. It turns out being altruistic or pursuing something greater than your self engages the brain’s reward systems.

If you pay in full every month, you’d pay no interest anyway, so choose a credit card on its rewards, such as the Power Cash Rewards card.

#8698. Should I Come Out of Retirement?

More than 60% of respondents in a 2026 Goldman Sachs survey of 5,106 working and retired Americans said they had taken work outside their primary job, most out of necessity rather than a wish for extra spending money. Nearly 70% had delayed a major financial goal.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability.

The news only makes matters worse. On Friday, October 30, we saw Nasdaq’s biggest 1-day drop since June 5, setting the internet ablaze with speculation. The index closed 7.8% below its October 6 record, though it was noted that the S&P 500 was only a few percent below its own record.

Then there’s inflation. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Pair that with continuing international conflicts on several fronts, and you’ve got the perfect storm of insecurity.

A National Institute on Retirement Security survey found that 80% of Americans say that the nation faces a retirement crisis and 61% worry they won’t be financially secure in retirement.

The respondents blamed inflation (73%) and market volatility (62%) as contributing factors, and 76% feared Social Security cuts if Congress fails to act.

A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Those who have already retired aren’t immune to these insecurities. The Goldman Sachs sample included 1,494 retirees aged 45 to 75. A market drop may also hurt more when you’re drawing from a portfolio than when you’re adding to it.

So, wondering if you should go back to work feels like a warranted question. Plenty of retirees take the leap back. Doctors go back too, though plenty of them say they don’t miss it. In a recent r/emergencymedicine thread, retired ED physicians were split on the question.

One, 3 years out, said he doesn’t miss it at all and still has the occasional nightmare. Another quit at 61 with no plan, misses the people and belonging to the group and keeps looking for work without luck.

1.5 million retirees reentered the workforce by March 2022.

We spend decades planning for the day we stop working. Then some of us stop, and a year or 2 later we’re checking job boards or answering calls from our old group. If that sounds like you, this article is for you.

Let’s take a look at the reasons many doctors feel the urge to un-retire, what going back to work in 2026 entails and the logistics of it all.

In case you missed it: Micro-retirements aren’t a shortcut to FIRE

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Money is the top reason many retirees choose to go back, so let’s start there. A recent survey found that 48% of working retirees said they needed the income, while 45% said they worked for social and emotional benefits.

Divide 1 year of spending by your portfolio. An example in T. Rowe Price’s example illustrates a 62-year-old with $900,000 who spends $65,000 a year.

That’s a 7.2% withdrawal rate. She has a 64% chance of not outliving her money if she retires at 62, a 91% chance at 65 and a 97% chance at 67.

Now let’s imagine a physician-specific version.

Say you have $2,500,000 and spend $150,000 a year before taxes. That’s a 6% withdrawal rate. A part-time job paying $60,000 would trim your withdrawals to $90,000, which is 3.6%.

You lower your rate by 2.4 percentage points without changing how you live. Of course, taxes will reduce that paycheck so ask your planner for a clearer outline.

One retired doctor said he saved about 30% of his take-home pay in his last years of full-time work, and his spending ended up around half of his colleagues’.

He could walk away any day, and his group knew it. That kind of freedom is helpful even after you return because you’re able to negotiate better when you don’t actually need the job.

Before you take a job, figure out whether the problem is your portfolio or your spending. If your withdrawal rate looks fine but spending still makes you uneasy, a concrete spending plan may help more than a paycheck. Ask your planner to set a monthly amount you can spend without second-guessing.

Working longer also helps in 2 other ways. You can delay account withdrawals as well as Social Security. Benefits grow 8% for every year you wait past full retirement age until you reach 70, while claiming at 62 cuts them by almost 30%.

Continuing to work also gives you more time to contribute to your retirement accounts. If your new employer offers a 401(k) or 403(b), the 2026 limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50 and older or $11,250 at ages 60 to 63.

It depends on whether you’ve claimed it and how old you are. If you haven’t claimed, going back to work is straightforward and your eventual monthly SS check will continue to increase.

If you claimed before full retirement age (FRA), the earnings test applies. In 2026, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 if you’re under FRA all year.

In the year you reach FRA, the limit rises to $65,160, and the agency withholds $1 for every $3 above it. Only earnings before the month you reach FRA count.

If your part-time schedule pays more than $24,480, expect withholding. The money isn’t gone for good, though. Social Security recalculates your benefit at FRA to credit the months it withheld.

Only wages and self-employment earnings count, so investment income doesn’t trigger withholding. Once you reach FRA, working doesn’t reduce your benefit.

You’ll also keep paying Social Security taxes on your paychecks. Higher earnings can also make more of your benefit taxable, so ask your tax preparer to estimate that too.

What if you changed your mind after claiming early? If you claimed before FRA, you have 12 months to withdraw your application. You must repay what you received, and Social Security then treats your record as if you never claimed at all.

Coverage before 65 costs far more in 2026 than it did in 2025 since the enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025.

KFF reports that a 60-year-old with a $65,000 income now pays an average of $10,389 more per year, or $865 per month. The subsidy cliff is also back which means above 400% of the poverty level (which is $62,600 for a single person in 2026), you lose the premium tax credit entirely.

On top of that, the ACA allows insurers to charge adults in their 60s up to 3 times what they charge adults in their 20s.

So a job with group health coverage may save you thousands of dollars a year because it skips the marketplace and the income cliff.

A working physician said that if he left medicine early, he’d take a flexible management job of about 25 hours a week mostly for the group insurance and the 401(k) match.

If you’re considering the same, ask HR what hours are required for benefits and when coverage starts, since each plan sets its own cutoff.

Medicare changes much of the picture. If you delayed Part B because you had coverage through your own or your spouse’s current job, you get an 8-month special enrollment period after that job or coverage ends.

If you miss it, you’ll have to pay 10% more for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B, for as long as you keep it. COBRA and retiree coverage don’t count for that exemption.

Keep in mind that Medicare generally pays first if the employer has fewer than 20 employees. So a small practice’s plan may pay second and you’d still need Part B.

Learn more: 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

Don’t count on getting your old job back.

An AARP survey of more than 3,500 people ages 50 and older found that 74% believe their age will be a barrier to getting hired, and 64% of workers 50 and older have seen or experienced age discrimination at work. That stigma is even worse for women.

Another AARP report found that 37% of workers 50 and older experienced subtle age discrimination during a job search in 2025, up from 30% in 2024. These surveys cover all fields, not only medicine, so ask recruiters in your specialty what they are seeing firsthand.

Think about what you want the next job to be. 24% of workers 50 and older planned a job change in 2025, so you won’t be the only one looking. If your retirement was driven mostly due to clinical work, teaching, consulting or chart review may suit you better than your old schedule.

We’ve already established that money drives about half of all unretirements. Boredom and a wish to help others drive many of the rest.

In an AARP survey, 18% of unretirees said boredom or a desire to stay active was their main reason for returning to work. For doctors, these sentiments start even before they leave.

In a Jackson Physician Search survey, 44% of physicians feared losing their sense of purpose in retirement and 39% feared boredom (money was still the top fear at 53%).

In CHG Healthcare’s 2024 survey, physicians who wanted to keep working felt that way because of a love of medicine (58%), social connections (57%) and concern for patients (39%). Others stated not feeling emotionally ready (47%), wanting to keep their lifestyle (35%) and fearing boredom or isolation (33%).

In Medscape’s 2025 retirement report, the top reason physicians gave for not retiring earlier was feeling they still had more to offer (62%), ahead of not having enough saved (45%). In the 2023 report, 46% expected retirement to feel like losing a part of their identity.

Retired and soon-to-retire ED physicians on Reddit offer a mixed bag of insights. One commenter who was 4 months from retiring expects to miss the ego boost of being a doctor. The one who quit at 61 with no plan misses colleagues and most of his patients, though not the fatigue of rotating shifts or the dread of sending home someone who should have stayed. Several said sleep and a normal daytime rhythm were the biggest change.

Retirement also changes what stresses you out. A 2025 Mayo Clinic review of physician well-being in retirement says that stress moves from work problems to personal ones, including professional identity, family, health and the loss of relationships.

The journal’s late-career paper urges physicians to plan for social and emotional needs along with finances. If you can’t picture your days without the work and the people, look at part-time options before you retire fully.

Give your first year in retirement a fair shake before you decide. People who leave long, consuming careers often describe a rocky start to retirement.

One user on Reddit said that it took about a year to stop feeling guilty about doing nothing. Another lasted 2 years, took a part-time job and has stayed 10 years. A third said the new job mattered to them mostly for the community, since all their friends still worked.

In case you missed it: The Nightmare Before Retirement: A Physician’s Cautionary Tale (2026 Edition)

If burnout pushed you out in the first place, the same job will push you out again. In 2026, burnout in healthcare is still running rampant.

Doximity’s May 2026 poll found that 82% of physicians say they’re overworked and 46% are considering early retirement because of it.

That number is up from 37% in 2025 and 21% in 2021. The jump is sharpest among women (54% in 2026 compared to 33% in 2023) and physicians ages 50 to 54 (56%, up from 35%).

Medscape’s 2026 burnout report corroborates this. 50% of male and 51% of female physicians say that their work causes their burnout, and 13%–14% are considering leaving medicine altogether.

In a MedCentral survey, 44% of physicians said they had considered leaving medical practice since the start of the year.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

A recent AMA study in The Permanente Journal looked at doctors who had already left and found that 971 clinically inactive physicians were typically 48.1 years old when they left clinical practice. Their top reasons were the hassle factor (44.7%), stress (44.5%), unrealistic patient demands (41.1%) and lack of professional satisfaction (38.4%).

Most doctors don’t plan to go cold turkey, however. In CHG Healthcare’s late-career survey, 63% of respondents said they’d rather work less than not work at all and 94% had at least slight interest in locum tenens work.

26% of physicians from a Weatherby Healthcare survey say that they are interested in locum tenens work. That’s 7 points higher than last year and the highest in 10 years.

If the actual reason behind your retirement still rings true or any of the reasons stated above give you a pause, you may want to reconsider jumping back into the workforce. Unless financial insecurity is twisting your arm, there’s no point in going back to something that already burned you out.

Fortunately, there are many other work options for physicians that don’t involve selling your soul. Locum tenens and expert witness work are popular ways for physicians to keep working.

Learn more: Physician Side Gigs That Actually Pay in 2026

Rules vary by state so check what’s needed where you live. Florida requires a reactivation fee, proof of continuing medical education (CME) for each year the license was inactive or retired, a health history and a financial responsibility form.

Pennsylvania requires full Board review and possibly proof of competency. According to the AAMC some states require a reentry program after an absence that averages about 3 years.

The ED physician who quit at 61 let his board certification lapse and said he now wishes he’d kept it, because it might have opened insurance work.

Another retired ED doctor commented that he dreamed for 2 years about working shifts without a license or malpractice cover. The roles you want to work in may or may not require these credentials so check before you make up your mind.

Most carriers give retiring physicians tail coverage free or at low cost. But some carriers may cancel that tail or charge a premium if you resume practice because when you return to clinical practice and receive pay or compensation for clinical work, you violate the retirement condition under which the tail fee was waived. Check with your provider.

The AMA warns that some physicians’ retirement income may change if they take paid work. Check your pension plan before you accept a role.

Of course, there’s no universal right answer and no rulebook that says you must make one permanent decision.

Start by being honest about why you feel the urge to return. If it’s your portfolio that’s got you worried, earning an income may give you some much-needed breathing room.

If you miss the people, intellectual challenge or sense of purpose, you might find what you’re looking for in a very different role.

But if you’re simply uncomfortable with having more time than you’ve ever had before, give yourself a little longer before dusting off your resume.

Most importantly, don’t let a bad week in the market convince you that decades of retirement planning have failed. Nor should you feel obliged to return to medicine because you miss being a physician. It’s okay to miss parts of your career without wanting the whole thing back.

And no matter what you decide, don’t let your credentials lapse. Your medical license and board certification represent years of hard work and keeping them active preserves options you may not realize you’ll want later.

Even if you’re 100% certain you’ll never practice again, give your future self the benefit of the doubt. You don’t have to use those credentials, but you might one day wish you still had them.

Also read: The Idea of “Retiring to” Something

It depends on your finances, personal goals and reasons for retiring. Returning to work can provide income, health insurance and social connections, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of the retirement you worked so hard to achieve.

The most common reasons include financial insecurity, boredom, loss of purpose, social isolation and missing the intellectual challenge of their former careers.

Yes. Retired physicians can return to clinical practice, provided they meet their state medical board’s licensing and reactivation requirements. They may also need to address CME, board certification and malpractice coverage.

Yes, if you claim Social Security before full retirement age. In 2026, benefits are withheld if your earnings exceed $24,480, or $65,160 in the year you reach full retirement age. The earnings test no longer applies once you reach FRA.

Keeping your medical license active preserves the option to return to clinical practice without going through the full reactivation process. Check your state’s renewal requirements and consider maintaining board certification, too.

There’s no set waiting period. Give yourself time to adjust to retirement and understand what’s driving your desire to return. If finances aren’t forcing the decision, consider giving retirement at least a year before making a move.

This was a really thoughtful look at a question with no single right answer. The withdrawal-rate example was especially clear — seeing how part-time work could bring a 6% rate down to 3.6% makes the math feel much less abstract. I also had not realized how much the 2026 ACA subsidy changes could push someone back toward a job with group coverage. The advice to keep a license and board certification active, even when you are sure you are done, seems like wise insurance for your future self.

#8696. Give a Store Gift Card, Not a Visa One – Skip the Purchase Fee

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Give a gift card for a store or restaurant the person you’re shopping for already uses. A Visa or Mastercard gift card costs several dollars more than it holds, and its last few dollars are hard to spend. A $50 card bought straight from the store or restaurant costs $50.

At Target, a $50 Visa or Mastercard gift card costs $55. The extra $5 is a purchase fee, and none of it reaches the person who opens the card.

Target’s fee on a $25 Visa gift card is $4, or 16% of the gift. In return, the card works almost anywhere. You don’t need that when you know where the person already spends, since a card for their usual store or restaurant goes to things they’d buy anyway.

The last few dollars on these cards are the other catch. Visa tells gift card holders to make sure the balance covers the whole purchase when they shop online. At a restaurant, Visa adds, the card may be checked for 20% more than the bill to cover the tip. A $45 dinner then needs $54 on the card, so a $50 card can be declined.

Choose the card by where they already spend: the grocery store a family shops at weekly, a commuter’s usual gas station, the streaming service they pay for, or the coffee shop they stop at before work. A card they’ll use up in a few visits never leaves a balance sitting in a drawer.

Buying on the brand’s own website keeps the card off store racks, where someone could tamper with it. If you buy one off a rack instead, check that the protective sticker is intact and the PIN on the back isn’t showing, as the Federal Trade Commission advises. Give the receipt along with the card, and keep a photo of both on your phone. The card number and receipt help you report a lost card or fraud to the company that issued it.

For someone whose favorite store you can’t name, put $50 in cash or a check in a holiday card instead of a Visa gift card. You skip the $5 fee, and they can spend every dollar.

#8694. Air France-KLM Flying Blue → Tahiti Business Class

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.
